title: The Vectosaur: Experience with an Expiration Date
content: After four decades of stalking mosquitoes, chasing tsetse flies, and waging slow, methodical war against arthropods capable of delivering disease, I sometimes feel like a relic. I am a vectosaur—a term coined by David Gorla, a good friend and prominent Argentinian entomologist. I collected vectors in Africa, mapped breeding sites in Asia, chased kissing bugs in South America, trudged through hurricane- damaged towns in the Caribbean, bartered for fuel in towns where gasoline was more precious than gold, and won the trust of community leaders whose cooperation meant the difference between containment and catastrophe. My tools were traps, paper maps, and patience. My currency was expe- rience—slowly earned and often paid for in blisters, missed family events, and occasional bouts of malaria. My memory is an atlas of insect habits and human mistakes. Yet, as any vectosaur can attest, the moment the contract ends (often after a polite phrase during a curt phone call that goes something like “we're moving in a different direction”) or the retirement papers are signed, your accumulated knowledge, sharpened over a lifetime, vanishes into the fog. It becomes irrelevant. Poof! Gone! The inbox goes quiet and the phone stops ringing. After decades of being “the one who knows,” you become the one they used to know.
